comment.value:
This paper introduces LITHOS, a novel dataset for automated petrography, a task with significant real-world applications but limited public resources. The authors contribute the largest available dataset featuring over 200k high-resolution image patches under two different polarization conditions (PPL and XPL), with more than 100k expert annotations across 25 mineral categories. 

Key contributions are: the establishment of the benchmark, a baseline model, release of the dataset with code and models.

The reviewers unanimously agree on the novelty of the dataset and its significance for the community. The paper is also clearly presented and results are reproducible. However, several concerns were raised. The most significant limitations identified were the dataset's limited geographical diversity and a pronounced class imbalance. One reviewer also argued for a more extensive comparison against a wider array of recent multimodal and single-modality architectures, finding the initial benchmarking somewhat limited.

The authors provided a good rebuttal and tried to address the reviewers' major concerns acknowledging the geographical and class-distribution limitations but convincingly framed them not as flaws, but as inherent, real-world challenges (e.g., long-tailed recognition) that make the benchmark more valuable. During the rebuttal phase additional experimental results were provided to strengthen the contribution.

author_final_remarks.value:
Dear ACs,

We would like to emphasize that LITHOS represents a significant contribution to the field of automated petrography. LITHOS is the largest and most diverse publicly available experimental framework for automated petrography, featuring 211,604 high-resolution RGB patches of polarized light and 105,802 expert-annotated grains across 25 mineral categories. This dataset captures both mineral classifications, grain geometry and orientation, providing critical spatial data that makes it an invaluable resource for advancing automated mineral classification.

The rebuttal session was very fruitful, as it allowed us to further strengthen the paper and the proposed benchmark. We appreciate the feedback, which helped us improve both the clarity and depth of our work. Based on the suggestions, we incorporated a Swin Transformer backbone as an additional architectural reference, strengthening the benchmark with another competitive model. This improvement, alongside the original models we tested, provides a more comprehensive evaluation and positions LITHOS as a robust, extensible foundation for future work in multimodal learning and scientific imaging. 

Empirically, LITHOS demonstrates that complementary polarization cues matter. Our dual-polarization fusion approach consistently outperforms single-modality training in both binary and multi-class settings. This work highlights the benefits of polarization synergy for mineral classification, showcasing how the integration of PPL and XPL data leads to superior model performance. We also provide essential computational metrics for all tested models, enabling cost-accuracy comparisons that facilitate reproducibility.

This work aligns closely with the NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks track, which encourages the development of high-quality, domain-grounded datasets that can stimulate new research directions and methodological advances. LITHOS presents a novel benchmark in a scientifically meaningful domain, inviting the community to tackle critical ML challenges, including multimodal fusion, class imbalance and long-tailed recognition, weak supervision, and interpretability. We believe LITHOS offers a valuable resource for the machine learning community to advance towards automated petrography. Given its comprehensive design, high-quality content, and potential to inspire further advancements in the field, we are confident that LITHOS is a valuable contribution to the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track.

We thank the reviewer for considering our response. Regarding his concern, we have designed our benchmarking pipeline to avoid data leakage and overfitting. We implemented a 2-fold cross-validation strategy at the thin section level. Each thin section is assigned exclusively to one of the two folds, ensuring that all patches from a given slide are grouped in either the training or validation split, but never both. This design preserves independence between folds and reflects a more realistic deployment scenario, where models are expected to generalize to unseen geological samples.  
We would also like to note that working with high-resolution petrographic images (24,786 × 16,259 pixels) poses a particular challenge: the large size of petrographic thin sections needs a patch-based approach. Direct training on entire slides is computationally infeasible and methodologically impractical for most ML architectures.

We thank the reviewer for carefully considering our responses. Regarding the comparisons, we would like to clarify that direct comparisons with previous petrography works were not feasible, as most prior approaches either targeted a different task (e.g., semantic segmentation) or did not release their implementation code. For the only related work with released code (Trans-SedNet), we found that the implementation could not be fully reproduced. These limitations highlight the gap in the field, and precisely for these reasons, our work paves the way towards automated petrography. By standardizing a benchmark with a comprehensive, annotated dataset and a robust evaluation framework, we aim to provide a valuable resource for assessing model performance and fostering further advancements in this domain. 

As for the methods related to polarization fusion mentioned in the initial review, most of those architectures rely on CNN- or Transformer-based modules. Taking into account that our benchmark focuses on image patch-level mineral classification, and to enrich our baselines and further strengthen the reproducibility and robustness of our work, we have additionally trained a Swin Transformer backbone. This model has been widely adopted in the computer vision community due to its hierarchical design and shifted-window attention mechanism, which enables strong performance across a range of classification and dense prediction tasks.

Regarding the performance of the Swin Transformer, we saw promising results of this method in our benchmark using a single polarization. We assessed its performance in both classification tasks. For both tasks, we present the metrics as the average and standard deviation across both folds. 

**Binary Classification Task**

For PPL, the Swin Transformer achieved an F1-score of 0.8455 ± 0.013, accuracy of 0.835 ± 0.014, recall of 0.8725 ± 0.016, and precision of 0.821 ± 0.011. 
For XPL, the model achieved an F1-score of 0.8555 ± 0.006, accuracy of 0.8435 ± 0.008, recall of 0.892 ± 0.001, and precision of 0.822 ± 0.013. 

**Multi-class Classification Task**

For PPL, the Swin Transformer achieved an F1-score of 0.422 ± 0.01, accuracy of 0.593 ± 0.025, recall of 0.4205 ± 0.016, and precision of 0.47 ± 0.006. 
For XPL, the model achieved an F1-score of 0.424 ± 0.011, accuracy of 0.604 ± 0.017, recall of 0.4205 ± 0.001, and precision of 0.4715 ± 0.039. 

These results underscore the benefits of our approach (LITHOS baseline), particularly the cross-attention mechanism integrated within our dual-decoder fusion module. The cross-attention allows for effective interaction between the feature maps extracted from each polarization modality, enabling richer representations and more accurate classification in both binary and multi-class classification tasks. 

Regarding the model complexity, the Swin Transformer has 86.9M trainable parameters and 17.1B FLOPs for both binary and multi-class tasks, with average inference times of 25.91ms for binary classification and 26.07ms for multi-class classification. Here is the updated table with model complexity data about all models: 

**Binary Classification**

**Swin Transformer:** 86.9M trainable / 86.9M total parameters / 17.1B FLOPs / 25.91 ms avg inference time 

**Multi-class Classification**

**Swin Transformer:** 86.9M trainable / 86.9M total parameters / 17.1B FLOPs / 26.07 ms avg inference time 

With this addition, our benchmark now includes two CNN-based baselines and two Transformer-based baselines, representing the two major architectural families in vision research, thus providing a solid foundation for future comparisons.

Petrography is a foundational discipline in geology, natural resource exploration, and planetary science. Its applications extend to critical areas such as mining for rare earth elements, evaluating materials for sustainable energy technologies, and even understanding the geological history of Earth and other planets. We believe this benchmark can serve as a valuable resource for developing generalizable multimodal learning techniques and encourage further contributions to this underexplored yet impactful application area. 

Finally, we would like to emphasize that the goal of this work aligns closely with the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track, which encourages the development of domain-grounded, high-quality datasets that can stimulate new research directions and methodological advances. The LITHOS benchmark addresses this by presenting a novel classification task in a scientifically meaningful domain and invites the community to tackle the following machine learning challenges: (i) Multimodal fusion, (ii) class imbalance and long-tailed distributions, (iii) weak supervision, and (iv) interpretability in a scientific domain that has been little studied by machine learning, such as petrography.

rebuttal.value:
Regarding the reviewer concerns:

**1. Relevance to NeurIPS**

We understand the reviewer’s concern regarding the connection between our domain-specific application (petrography) and the broader NeurIPS community. Our benchmark aligns with the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track, which is intended for high-quality, domain-grounded datasets that can drive progress in machine learning research.
Our work provides:
- A large-scale, dual-modality benchmark that introduces a new, underexplored computer vision task: mineral classification from polarized optical microscopy.
- A well-structured evaluation protocol (binary and multi-class), and
- An open, reproducible baseline using dual-encoder attention-based fusion, aligned with current multimodal learning paradigms.

As emphasized by the D&B track, impactful datasets should offer challenges that can inspire algorithmic innovation and generalizable insights. In our case, the LITHOS benchmark invites the machine learning community to develop methods that handle:
- Multimodal fusion of structured visual signals (plane- and cross-polarized images),
- Class imbalance and long-tailed distributions,
- Weak supervision via structured annotations (major and minor axes instead of full masks), and
- Interpretability challenges in a scientific domain that has been little studied, such as petrography.

**2. Insights about experimentation**

We appreciate the reviewer’s interest in understanding which architectural components are responsible for the performance gains of our LITHOS Baseline.
The core insight of our architecture is that the improvement does not stem from training deeper or larger models end-to-end. In fact, our two ViT encoders, which specialize in plane-polarized (PPL) and cross-polarized (XPL) images, are frozen during training. 

Therefore:
- The observed performance gains do not result from ViT pretraining alone (as the same pretrained ViTs are used in the single-modality baselines), and
- The gains are not due to having more trainable parameters, since only ~10% of the full model is updated.
Instead, our hypothesis is that the improvement primarily stems from the cross-attention mechanisms in our dual-decoder fusion module, which enables interaction between the feature maps extracted from each polarization modality. This architecture encourages the model to learn how features observed under PPL complement or refine those seen under XPL, and vice versa. In essence, the model is learning to "attend across polarizations" rather than just across image patches.

Regarding the reviewer concerns:

**Limited clarity:** We thank the reviewer for highlighting the lack of explanation of petrography-specific terms. We will address this in the final version by refining definitions and providing brief clarifications where necessary. Regarding the specific questions raised, a mineral grain refers to an individual crystal or crystal fragment of a mineral that is visually distinguishable in a thin section based on its optical properties, such as color, relief, cleavage, and birefringence, when observed under a petrographic microscope. Additionally, the samples were annotated by a team of six experts from the Geology Department at Universidad de los Andes, Colombia. To ensure consistency and accuracy, each annotation underwent a secondary review. Finally, polarization imaging was conducted using a standard petrographic microscope, where the thin section is placed on the microscope stage (probe location). In this type of microscope, a polarizer is placed below the sample, and an analyzer is placed above it. By rotating either the stage or the polarizing filters, one can capture images in plane-polarized light (PPL) and cross-polarized light (XPL).

**Number of images:** The 2,860 images per thin section refer to the number of regions captured during the scanning process. However, these image regions are subsequently stitched together to construct a single high-resolution mosaic (24,786 × 16,259 pixels) for each thin section. Regarding the reviewer concerns:

**1. Multimodal fusion methods**

We appreciate the suggestion to consider these advanced multimodal fusion methods. However, our benchmark focuses on mineral classification at the image patch level, whereas the cited methods are primarily designed for semantic segmentation tasks that output pixel-wise labels. Incorporating segmentation frameworks (which rely on semantic masks or pixel-level supervision) is not directly applicable to our classification setup. Adapting those methods would require significant modifications (e.g., converting segmentation outputs to a single label or training on different ground truth), which fall outside the scope of this benchmark paper. We chose to concentrate on image-level classification because our dataset’s primary annotation is a mineral label per image patch (with associated grain attributes), not full segmentation masks. The goal of our benchmark is to establish baseline performance on mineral identification using polarized images. Including segmentation models (such as PGSNet and ACNet) would not yield a meaningful comparison, as they are designed to solve a different problem. That said, we will clarify this distinction in the final version. 

**2. Qualitative analysis**
 
We agree that thorough ablation and qualitative analysis are important. In the current submission, we have already included an ablation study on the polarization modalities in Tables 2 and 3. Specifically, we evaluated the performance of the Vision Transformer (ViT) using only plane-polarized light (PPL) images and only cross-polarized light (XPL) images independently, and then compared these to our proposed LITHOS dual-polarization baseline (which uses both PPL and XPL). This experiment demonstrates the benefit of combining both polarization modalities. For both the binary classification task and the multi-class task, our LITHOS baseline outperforms the single-modality models (as shown by higher accuracy and F1-score in Tables 2 and 3). We will ensure that these results are highlighted more clearly in the final version, as they directly validate the contribution of our polarization fusion approach. 
Regarding qualitative results, we acknowledge the reviewer's interest in seeing examples. In the original submission, due to space constraints, we focused on quantitative results and included some aggregate visualizations (e.g., per-class precision-recall curves in the supplementary material). In the final version, we will add qualitative illustrations to provide more insight into the model’s behavior. For instance, we can include a figure with example image patches under PPL and XPL, showing the model’s predictions vs. ground truth. This could highlight cases where the dual-polarization model correctly identifies minerals that single-polarization models misclassify.

**3. Computational complexity** 

We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. In the current version of the paper, we provide the total number of parameters for our proposed LITHOS Baseline, but we acknowledge that a more comprehensive complexity analysis, including the parameter counts of all baselines, would strengthen the work. To address this, we summarize below the number of trainable and total parameters for each model evaluated in both the binary and multi-class classification settings, along with additional computational metrics such as FLOPs and average inference time:

**Binary classification (2 classes):**

·       **ViT:** 303M trainable / 303M total parameters / 59.7B FLOPs / 17.45 ms avg inference time

·       **GoogLeNet:** 5M trainable / 5M total parameters / 1.51B FLOPs / 5.18 ms avg inference time

·       **ResNet:** 23M trainable / 23M total parameters / 4.14B FLOPs / 4.46 ms avg inference time

·       **LITHOS Baseline:** 67M trainable / 673M total parameters / 133.26B FLOPs / 40.18 ms avg inference time

**Multi-class classification (25 classes):**

·       **ViT:** 303M trainable / 303M total parameters / 59.7B FLOPs / 17.60 ms avg inference time

·       **GoogLeNet:** 5M trainable / 5M total parameters / 1.51B FLOPs / 5.18 ms avg inference time

·       **ResNet:** 23M trainable / 23M total parameters / 4.14B FLOPs / 4.46 ms avg inference time

·       **LITHOS Baseline:** 67M trainable / 673M total parameters / 133.28B FLOPs / 40.18 ms avg inference time

The LITHOS Baseline has a large total parameter count and a high number of FLOPs compared to the other baselines, due to its dual ViT encoders. However, these encoders are kept frozen during training, meaning only ~10% of the parameters are updated. This design reduces the effective training cost and memory consumption while leveraging strong, pretrained features from each polarization stream, which is key to improving classification performance. We will include these parameter counts and computational metrics in the final version to provide a clearer and more comprehensive analysis of the model's computational complexity.

**4. Benchmark and additional methods** 

We understand the reviewer’s interest in seeing a broader range of classification models. Our strategy in this benchmark was to include a focused set of strong, representative baselines rather than an exhaustive evaluation of architectures. In Tables 2 and 3, we reported results for ResNet (a canonical CNN model), GoogLeNet (another influential CNN with a different design), and ViT (a modern Transformer-based classifier). These three were chosen as standard and diverse baselines from two major model families, to ensure robust and reproducible comparisons. While ResNet and GoogLeNet cover classic convolutional network designs, ViT represents the transformer family, together providing a baseline spectrum for the community to reference. Moreover, for the final version, we will add another transformer-based method for comparison purposes. This addition will further enrich the evaluation and provide the community with more reference points for transformer-based approaches.
We agree that exploring other architectures is valuable for future work. We will mention in the revised text that our benchmark is extensible: researchers can easily plug in other backbone models to evaluate on LITHOS. In fact, since we will be releasing the dataset and code, the community will be able to test additional networks under the same conditions.

We would like to highlight that our benchmark aligns with the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track, which is intended for high-quality, domain-grounded datasets that can drive progress in machine learning research.
Our work provides:
- A large-scale, dual-modality benchmark that introduces a new, underexplored computer vision task: mineral classification from polarized optical microscopy.
- A well-structured evaluation protocol (binary and multi-class), and
- An open, reproducible baseline using dual-encoder attention-based fusion, aligned with current multimodal learning paradigms.

As emphasized by the D&B track, impactful datasets should offer challenges that can inspire algorithmic innovation and generalizable insights. In our case, the LITHOS benchmark invites the machine learning community to develop methods that handle:
- Multimodal fusion of structured visual signals (plane- and cross-polarized images),
- Class imbalance and long-tailed distributions,
- Weak supervision via structured annotations (major and minor axes instead of full masks), and
- Interpretability challenges in a scientific domain that has been little studied, such as petrography.

We appreciate the comment regarding the imbalance in class representation within our dataset. As noted, quartz and its subtypes dominate the collection, reflecting their natural abundance in many geological settings. Our intention in preserving this long-tail distribution was to ensure the dataset remains representative of real-world mineralogical compositions, particularly in applications relevant to sustainable soil and rock exploration. Rather than applying artificial balancing strategies, we believe that decisions regarding augmentation or rebalancing are best made based on the specific needs of the application and the objectives of the model. Our focus was on collecting a representative dataset and establishing a baseline that can serve as a foundation for future work, promoting continued progress towards automated petrography.
We acknowledge that this imbalance poses challenges for multi-class classification and may limit model performance in rarer mineral categories. Therefore, we conducted a preliminary per-class performance analysis (Lines 261–276, Fig. 6), which highlights both the impact of class frequency and the influence of distinct visual patterns. For instance, classes like Foraminifer and Red Algae achieve relatively strong performance despite their rarity, likely due to their highly recognizable biological structures. In contrast, broad or visually inconsistent classes such as Heavy Mineral and Other exhibit lower F1-scores, as do fine-grained or visually overlapping classes such as Feldspar and Plagioclase. This suggests that model performance is not solely dictated by class frequency but also by the clarity and consistency of visual features under polarized light. We will expand this per-class analysis in the final version of our paper.

summary.value: The LITHOS dataset is the largest and most comprehensive publicly available resource for automated petrography, comprising 211,604 high-resolution RGB image patches and 105,802 expert-annotated mineral grains across 25 mineral categories, captured under both plane-polarized and cross-polarized light. Derived from 580 thin sections of Colombian soils, the dataset includes detailed annotations such as mineral class, spatial coordinates, and grain geometry using vector paths. Accompanying this dataset, the authors introduce the LITHOS Benchmark for both binary and multi-class classification tasks, along with a transformer-based dual-encoder model that effectively leverages dual-polarization inputs to outperform single-modality baselines. The framework is designed to support reproducible research and advance the development of AI-driven mineral identification tools.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. LITHOS is the largest petrography dataset to date, with 211,000+ image patches and 105,000+ expert-labeled grains, including spatial and geometric data for rich feature learning.
2. It introduces paired PPL/XPL imaging and a dual-encoder transformer that outperforms single-modality models, supported by a robust benchmark for binary and multi-class tasks.

Although a binary classification task partially mitigates this issue, the multi-class setup remains significantly imbalanced.

summary.value: This paper introduces LITHOS, a large-scale dataset and benchmark for automated petrography, comprising over 200,000 high-resolution polarized thin-section images annotated into 25 mineral classes. The authors also propose a dual-encoder transformer architecture that fuses plane- and cross-polarized views, demonstrating improved performance over single-modality baselines. The dataset, code, and pretrained models are planned for public release.

strengths_contributions.value:

Compared to prior resources, the dataset is orders of magnitude larger and includes rich annotations (e.g., mineral labels, geometric axes), which will likely become an essential reference for the community.

summary.value: This paper proposed the LITHOS dataset, which serves as a large-scale image for automated petrography. The dataset has two polarization conditions. The associated benchmark has been established. A dual-encoder transformer architecture is created to leverage paired PPL and XPL views. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating complementary polarization information.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. A large-scale polarization-driven automated petrography dataset is established with the associated benchmark.
2. The dual-encoder transformer model effectively incorporates complementary polarization cues.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. More polarization-driven methods like polarization-driven semantic segmentation, ShareMLP, PGSNet, the dual-encoder CMX, CMNeXt, ACNet, GeminiFusion, and TokenFusion could be compared to illustrate the superiority of the proposed model and discussed in detail.
2. More detailed ablations and parameter analyses could be done to look into the effects of PPX, XPL, and other polarization information representations for automated petrography. The corresponding qualitative analyses could be added.
3. The computational complexity of the established dual-encoder model could be analyzed by presenting its results like FLOPs/MACs, the number of parameters, running time, and memory requirements.
4. More single-modality backbone classification methods should be benchmarked on the dataset, which could be added to Tables 2 and 3.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: The reviewer would like to thank the authors for the response, which helps to clarify some concerns. summary.value: The authors contribute a novel dataset for petrography, the scientific classification of rocks, containing 580 thin sections with multiple 2860 raw patches taken per section, resulting 105,802 patches of annotated mineral grains, with two images each. The authors then train various neural network architectures on the data, and provide a baseline for classification on this benchmark.

strengths_contributions.value:
The work is generally well-written, and provides a digestible overview of the general field of petrography, including (mostly) proper placement among related works.

Petrography is a field that the machine learning community has had limited exposure to, and creating in-roads between the two communities may pave the way for fruitful cross-pollination and collaboration.

The efforts behind curating and producing this dataset containing novel data appears to be significant, requiring ~1700 hours of data collection and processing.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Limited clarity: While the paper is generally well written, there were certain parts I found unclear. For example, certain terminology and experimental setups specific to geology and petrography were not well discussed in the main paper or the supplementary. (What are mineral grains? Who annotates the samples? How is polarization photography conducted?) 

More specifically, one detail I found confusing was that the authors note that there were approximately 2860 images captured per thin section, and that there were 580 thin sections. This should result in ~1.6 million total images, but only 211,604 images were ultimately included in the dataset. Was there a filtering procedure on the total images captured?

Lower diversity: The dataset is ultimately composed of 580 thin sections obtained from Colombian soil, processed and photographed via a single homogenous procedure, and annotated via a single annotation software pipeline. While I do not want to trivialize the level of scale of this data collection effort, I have concerns about the generalizability of the results here.

Limited comparisons: While the authors compare several architectures for petrographic classification on the contributed dataset, there were no comparisons to models from related works.

I found that Table 1 was somewhat misleading, as for some works, the total number of thin sections (i.e. Sener et. al, 600 sections) was compared to the number of image patches of the present dataset (211,604) rather than the number of thin sections in the present dataset (580 sections).

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: I thank the authors for their clear response. The two-fold cross validation strategy alleviates some of my concerns, and I hope the authors will be able to update the work with model performance under this evaluation scheme. I am still concerned about correlation and batch effect across patches due to the fact that many patches come from the same thin section. In spite of these reservations, I do believe this work introduces a novel and scientifically interesting dataset / problem to the broader ML community, and maintain my positive rating.

summary.value: This paper introduces LITHOS dataset that includes 211k RGB patches of polarized images and 105k expert-annotated grains in 25 mineral categories. The LITHOS dataset is larger than previous work. Various numbers of DL architectures are benchmarked on the dataset. Final results show that the dual-encoder baseline has better performance than Resnet, Googlenet, and single-encoder ViT.

strengths_contributions.value:
(1) The collected dataset contains 211k images and 105k grains, which is much larger than previous work. For example, Ma et al.[34] only has1.8k images and 19k grains.

(2) The paper is well written and easy to follow.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Sorry that this submission about petrography is not in my research area.
(1) I agree that this petrography is much larger and more comprehensive than previous works, as shown in Table 1.
My largest consideration is its relevance to Neural Information Processing.

(2) Experiments in Table 2 show that the dual-encoder has better performance than Resnet, Googlenet, and ViT. Lines 261 to 276 analyze the results from the view of mineral categories. What insights about neural learning can we learn from these experiments? Does the improvement of the LITHOS baseline come from the attention operator, vit pretraining, or larger parameters?

abstract.value: Petrography is a branch of geology that analyzes the mineralogical composition of rocks from microscopical thin section samples. It is essential for understanding rock properties across geology, archaeology, engineering, mineral exploration, and the oil industry. However, petrography is a labor-intensive task requiring experts to conduct detailed visual examinations of thin section samples through optical polarization microscopes, thus hampering scalability and highlighting the need for automated techniques. To address this challenge, we introduce the Large-scale Imaging and Thin section Optical-polarization Set (LITHOS), the largest and most diverse publicly available experimental framework for automated petrography. LITHOS includes 211,604 high-resolution RGB patches of polarized light and 105,802 expert-annotated grains across 25 mineral categories. Each annotation consists of the mineral class, spatial coordinates, and expert-defined major and minor axes represented as intersecting vector paths, capturing grain geometry and orientation. We evaluate multiple deep learning techniques for mineral classification in LITHOS and propose a dual-encoder transformer architecture that integrates both polarization modalities as a strong baseline for future reference. Our method consistently outperforms single-polarization models, demonstrating the value of polarization synergy in mineral classification. We have made the LITHOS Benchmark publicly available, comprising our dataset, code, and pretrained models, to foster reproducibility and further research in automated petrographic analysis.
